concept: Photoelectric effect as evidence for photons
prompt: State two observations of the photoelectric effect that the wave model of light cannot explain, and explain how the photon model accounts for them.
markscheme:
No emission below a threshold frequency, however intense the light **(A1)**; emission is instantaneous even at very low intensity **(A1)**

Each electron absorbs one photon of energy $hf$; if $hf<\Phi$ no electron escapes, and a single photon can release an electron immediately **(R1)**

prompt: Light below the threshold frequency shines on a metal. If its intensity is doubled:
options: photoelectrons are emitted with low energy
twice as many photoelectrons are emitted
photoelectrons are emitted after a delay
markscheme: **D.** Doubling intensity doubles the number of photons but not the energy of each, which is still below the work function.

prompt:
Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on sodium, whose work function is 2.3 eV. ($h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)

**(a)** Calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV. **[2]**

**(b)** Calculate the threshold frequency of sodium. **[1]**
Describe an experiment that shows electrons have wave properties.
markscheme: Electrons accelerated through a few kV pass through a thin crystalline (graphite) film **(A1)**; concentric rings appear on a fluorescent screen — a diffraction pattern, which only waves produce, with ring size consistent with $\lambda=\frac hp$ **(R1)**

prompt: Which phenomenon is evidence for the **particle** nature of light?
markscheme: **C.** Diffraction, interference and polarisation are wave behaviours; the photoelectric effect (and Compton scattering) need photons.

prompt:
**(a)** Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through 100 V. ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg) ($h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C) **[2]**

**(b)** Explain why a 0.16 kg ball moving at $30\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ shows no wave behaviour. **[1]**
markscheme:
**(a)** $p=\sqrt{2m_eeV}=5.4\times10^{-24}\ \text{kg m s}^{-1}$ **(A1)**; $\lambda=\dfrac hp=1.2\times10^{-10}$ m — similar to atomic spacings, so electrons diffract off crystals **(A1)**

**(b)** $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{mv}\approx1.4\times10^{-34}$ m, far too small to diffract from any real gap **(R1)**

prompt: Explain why Compton scattering is evidence for the particle nature of light.
markscheme: X-ray photons scattered by electrons emerge with a longer wavelength that depends on the scattering angle **(A1)**; this matches a collision of a particle with momentum $\frac h\lambda$ and an electron, conserving energy and momentum — a wave model predicts no wavelength change **(R1)**

prompt: After a photon scatters off a free electron, the photon's:
markscheme: **B.** The photon gives some energy to the recoiling electron, so its energy falls and its wavelength increases; its speed is still $c$.

prompt: X-rays of wavelength 0.0710 nm are scattered through $90^{\circ}$ by electrons. Calculate the scattered wavelength. ($m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg) ($h=6.63\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=3.00\times10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, $e=1.60\times10^{-19}$ C)
